I consider Joseph Schlesinger to be a very reputable correspondent. He wrote:
Canada and the United States have both been going through tough times the past three years with high unemployment, increasing poverty and strained budgets.
But there is a major difference in how the two countries have dealt with the victims of the hard times.
Call it the Compassion Difference.
Paraphrasing the President of the United States, he has said that a lot of people sleep out at nights because they choose to do so. A former assistant to the President, the Attorney General of the United States, says that people go to soup kitchens to eat because it is cheaper that way. This shows a lack of compassion and there have been large cuts in these areas.
One would not think that these cuts would have created growing deficits in the United States. There were large tax cuts for people earning $80,000, for instance, which amounted to $15,000; but for people earning under $10,000, it amounted to $240 per year. The congressional budget office tells us that if defence expenditure increases and tax cuts had not been brought in, the United States would have no deficit by next year. That is what happens under a very conservative government, Mr. Speaker.
I cannot tell whether the Official Opposition would do the same thing if it formed the government but it seems as if it is indicating it would. That gives me great concern about what would happen to pensions, family allowances and health services, for instance. The Tories talk about cutting back on such things and increasing defence spending. They sound exactly like President Reagan.
This Budget brought in some very important programs. A lot of Canadians are afraid for the future and in some areas the fear is legitimate. Contrary to what I see in the United States, I see in this Budget an attempt to eliminate some of the worst fears. I believe the worst fear which Canadians can have in an economic sense is the fear that when one retires there will not be enough money to keep oneself going. That is particularly the case with private pension plans where very often when the husband dies, he being the person who worked and who put money into a pension plan, the wife receives nothing, or two years of benefit or something of that nature. We are saying we must get these private pension plans working. We must make sure that people have good incomes after retirement. It is very important that people be secure. These pensions must be indexed so that people can continue to live in a decent way. This kind of thinking is very different from what I see of the Reagan government in the United States, and it is different from what I believe is going to happen if those people opposite come into power.
There is another area where there has been a good deal of concern over the past few years. We have had a lot of cases in Thunder Bay where people buy a house, put down a nice down payment and are managing very well. Then all of a sudden interest rates climb. They have to renew their mortgages and they are caught. Perhaps one member of the family loses a job and they cannot make the payments. As a result, they lose their home.
We have fought very hard for a solution in my own constituency, and I commend the people in my office particularly, who have written very many letters about this kind of situation. We are now putting a plan into action which will give protection to Canadian home owners so that they will be secure in the knowledge that their mortgage will have, more or less, a fixed interest rate. These are the kinds of things which a compassionate government does, and which we have been doing. But I am very much afraid, and I believe Canadians are very much afraid, that in the future, if the government changes, this will not be the case.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak this afternoon on Bill C-21, an Act to provide borrowing authority. I feel a great deal of compassion-and I would like to express it at this time-for those members of the Government, such as the previous speak-
March 7, 1984

er from Thunder Bay, who must attempt to defend this borrowing authority Bill. That Hon. Member indeed danced around in a vacuum and really gave no explanation, as far as I am concerned, for the horrendous debt which this Bill intends to impose on the people of Canada.
Bill C-21 is a short Bill; it has three paragraphs. But I do not want Hon. Members of this House, or the people of Canada, to be misled by its shortness into believing that Bill C-21 is insignificant, because this Bill packs an immense wallop. It has enough of a wallop to bankrupt most of the small businesses of this country when the rippling effect is finally felt throughout the system in high interest rates and inflation. It has a wallop big enough to destroy the middle class in this country when the rippling effect of inflation and high interest rates is felt, and that is bound to occur when this Bill hits the money markets. I tell you, Sir, that no one in Canada should ignore this "small" Bill because we and our children are going to be living with it for a long time.
This Bill provides to Canadians, to this House, the philosophy of the Liberal Party starting from 1968 when this Government came into power. The Liberal philosophy is reflected in this borrowing Bill because its philosophy is to overspend- overspend yesterday, overspend today and overspend tomorrow.
What do I mean by overspending? My definition of spending is when government taxes people and uses that money for the operation of government. Overspending is when government does not have any money and spends anyway and must borrow outside the country. That is the Liberal Government philosophy-overspending. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it has been so successful in that philosophy it has out-NDPed the NDP. That poor Party has no place to go now because the Liberals have taken over its socialist position of heavy spending.
This Government's spending since 1968 is well detailed as a percentage of the Gross National Product, and I would like to inform you, Mr. Speaker, that this is on a national accounts basis. My figures do not seem to agree with some of the other figures which have been bandied about, particularly by the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) who spoke for the New Democratic Party. We had a lot of humbug from Humboldt. My figures show, and I believe these are accurate figures, that in 1968-1969 we were spending 17.4 per cent of the Gross National Product. That figure has increased steadily. The only time it showed a decrease was during the period when the Conservatives were in power. That was in 1979-1980, I believe, and the figure decreased by one percentage point that one year. In the previous year government spent 21.3 per cent of the Gross National Product. The following year when the Conservatives were in power, it was 20.7 per cent. The year after when the Liberals again became the Government, spending went up to 21.2 per cent, and today it is 25 per cent. Spending is going up, up, up, and there is no indication it will go down.
That is an example of the Liberal Government's philosophy. We have a Budget of $100 billion. We have an annual deficit of $30 billion. We have a total deficit of some $180 billion at
Borrowing Authority Act
the end of this year. Not very many people can comprehend $180 billion. However, I believe everyone can comprehend $6,000 to $7,000 a year, and that is the debt which every child born today is burdened with. That is our children's heritage because of the overspending of the Liberal Government over the past number of years. The minute a child is brought into this world he or she owes a debt of $7,000. How it is going to be paid is really a good question.
What has concerned me, and I believe what concerns a lot of Canadians, is how can anyone spend so much money? How can one overspend to the extent of $30 billion a year? We have been provided with some very good examples and I do not intend to go into all of them, but I would like to mention a few which the average Canadian can understand. However, first of all, I would like to tell the average Canadian that the deficit of $30 billion is probably not an exact figure. I will quote what the Auditor General said in his report about that deficit;
The increase in the national debt is important to all Canadians. Parliamentarians have the need-and all Canadians the right-to know the actual deficit, the actual debt as precisely as can be stated.
He continues, and this is the important part:
My opinion on the Financial Statements of the Government of Canada illustrates that those amounts would differ by many billions of dollars from what is presented-
That is the $30 billion figure. So we are not even getting the facts on this horrendous $30 billion annual deficit. As I was saying, how do you overspend that kind of money, Mr. Speaker? Well, let us go to something Canadians can understand, the Auditor General's report. He talks about a horror story in New Brunswick involving the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with Bill C-21, the Government is asking the House for permission to borrow the monies it needs
for the proper administration, and I emphasize the words proper administration, Mr. Speaker, of the country's business.
I do not intend to elaborate on the basis for this request, which is fair and reasonable, since I believe my learned colleague from Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) already did so very successfully. I would rather discuss a number of situations that prevail in my riding as they do generally across Canada, and that justify this request for supplementary borrowing authority. That the Government is asking a little more than it needs merely proves that the Government would rather be safe than sorry. The affairs of state must be administered with an eye to what the future may hold in store, and I think it is quite normal that the Government should ask the House for sufficient borrowing authority to cover its requirements.
I think it is hardly necessary to recall the state of the economy in preceding years, especially since 1981, or perhaps towards the end of 1980 and the beginning of 1981. The economic situation has become extremely difficult, and at the same time it has been necessary for the Government to protect jobs and especially to plan ahead for new generations entering the labour market. When I say that we should open up labour market opportunities, I should add that every effort ought to be made to bring back into the labour market those of our fellow Canadians who have lost their jobs.
I would like to quote a few figures on the amounts of money earmarked by the Government to meet the needs of the people in a region such as mine. If we add up all the money spent not so long ago in Eastern Quebec in particular on unemployment insurance and social assistance, we find that the Canadian Government has been paying out $1 million every day. It seems to me that, in such circumstances, any intelligent person would eventually wonder whether those funds might be expended in a more productive and constructive way than keeping people idle and giving them unemployment insurance benefits or social welfare hand-outs. That is why we have set up very worthwhile programs by using the funds allocated under the provisions of Unemployment Insurance Act Section 38.
Mr. Speaker, a significant part of Quebec forests cover my region-the entire territory of Temiscouata, Kamouraska, Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe-and everyone knows that it has been extensively ravaged by the spruce budworm. Thanks to the funds made available through unemployment insurance under Section 38 of the Act, we were able to carry out major reforestation and silviculture projects, to the extent that our forests have been given a new lease on life. Millions of young trees were planted, and all those projects have kept Canadians at work to ensure a much brighter future for ourselves and our children. It may have cost a little more than paying unemployment insurance benefits, but the Government and various groups of people put in additional funds to see the projects
March 7, 1984

through under those programs, and even some companies and institutions pitched in so that a great many people, thousands of my fellow citizens, have been able to earn an honest living while doing something useful for the community. Our intention is to maintain those programs and to encourage people to undertake worthwhile projects under them.
With respect to social welfare, we realize now that it is becoming increasingly imperative for the well-being of our community and Canada as a whole to make sure that people who are penalized because they lack adequate training or face job shortages can benefit from some of those programs with a view to becoming active in their community and eventually finding gainful employment.
In this regard, Hon. Members learned last week that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) had signed an agreement with the Quebec Minister of Manpower and Employment Security under which the Canadian Government agreed to increase its contribution by about $60 million over two years to enhance the social assistance program.
Now let us see how these funds will be used to improve the welfare of all the young people who will benefit from them, and I mention young people because this program is intended for those under 30. In addition to receiving the social assistance to which they are entitled, they will be getting an additional amount of $150 a month. Three avenues will then open to them. First, they may continue their secondary or even postsecondary education. They may also gain experience in the workplace by way of contacts with businesses and non-profit organizations, or alternatively institutions will be able to use the services of these young people who will then be gaining an extremely important experience in the workplace. In addition, these young people will be able to take part in projects to meet the needs of the community.
Mr. Speaker, you know as well as I do how extremely important it is to see that this whole section of our population, namely our young people under 30, is integrated as much as possible into what is usually considered a normal society, in other words, people who have as many opportunities to work as possible. However, you also know that in view of the deterioration of the economic situation, there have been serious problems; and if we add to this the thrust of technological changes and everything that will come up in the future, some of our fellow citizens are ill-prepared to take up these new challenges. The program I have just described and on which the federal and provincial Ministers have agreed will offer thousands of young people a very interesting opportunity to improve themselves by taking part in creative and innovative projects for the community.
I also want to deal with certain programs administered by the Department of Employment and Immigration. As I was saying, a number of young men and women have to return to the labour market and the Department of Employment and Immigration is offering them some very useful programs.

Programs such as the Youth Job Corps and Career-Access even allow these young people to submit their own projects to the Department and do what they really want.
In particular, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw your attention to a program developed by Employment and Immigration Canada and administered by the Department of National Defence. I do not believe that it is out of order for me to describe the use that is made of the tax dollars paid by the Canadian people and of the funds for which the Government requests some borrowing authority. In addition to the vast amounts used for the financing of established programs, particularly health and education, there are a number of programs which are necessary and which must be maintained. Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw your attention more particularly to a program which I find extremely interesting for young people. You do remember that the Department of National Defence was asked to develop and implement a whole system of training and employment for some 5000 young people, in its various centres in Canada. The goal we had in mind was to give these young people a special but rewarding training and at the same time an opportunity to explore some trades or professions otherwise unfamiliar to them. In my own area, in Rimouski, enlistment is done at the recruitment centres of National Defence, and 75 young people have taken advantage of that program. They have been with National Defence for a year now.
In the Sept-Iles area where employment problems are very serious, 75 young people have joined the program. In the Atlantic area, for example, 1,057 young people are with National Defence, 1,247 in the Quebec region, 1,809 in central Canada or Ontario, 1,103 in Western Canada. This means that 5,216 young men and women are with National Defence benefitting from a most interesting personal training. In addition, they can learn several trades in those various centres. For instance, those young people can find themselves in the bases in Cornwallis, St. John, Petawawa, Valcartier, Calgary, and so on, and get training in various skills or professions such as administration and finance, the postal service, all technical services. Training can be had in nearly all the trades connected with the navy, even in music, which is not to be disdained. This means that many thousands of young people are now availing themselves of a special program that is worthwhile, both for National Defence and society in general. I remember some parents who told me at home: Perhaps if you had fewer programs or no programs for the young, the Solicitor General or the Minister of Justice in some provinces might have to expand their facilities. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the programs now being offered by the Government of Canada, to women and young people in education or manpower training or the retraining programs for adults are absolutely vital and are only an addition to the normal services the Government of Canada should provide to all Canadians. In the light of the current situation, of course this is expensive. It is extremely

March 7, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
costly to ensure that the greatest possible number of people can earn a decent living, making a contribution to society rather than living off it. But it must be recognized that the monies invested in training or adult education are also an asset to us, they are an investment, and it seems to me that it would be niggardly at this point to suggest the funds are being misused or misspent by the Canadian Government. The economic situation we have been going through has been extremely difficult, not only financially, but also, as we know, it has created serious social problems for many individuals and families. In a region such as Eastern Quebec where at one point the unemployment rate almost reached 50 per cent between 1981 and 1982, while the current rate is still 21 to 22 per cent, we have a responsibility in my view to alleviate the hardships or despair which the lack of jobs might cause to many people.
The programs I have just referred to, such as welfare which was once considered as somewhat degrading for the people who are entitled to it, are now enriched because education has been added. People who want to make the effort will be able to go back to school, or train on the job or acquire work experience and do community work. It is simply a matter of giving Canadians, especially young men and women, an opportunity to upgrade their training and get better jobs. They feel more integrated when they can be positively and constructively involved. Like all of us, they now feel they are contributing to building this country while helping their fellow Canadians and hoping that their experiences will enable them to fulfil their role as citizens. This has been our goal when designing stimulating, innovative and flexible programs which will provide young men and women with the opportunity to use their imagination in making the best possible contribution to their community. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will support the Government's request for authorization to borrow sufficient funds, because as I said earlier, this money is needed to effectively manage public affairs in the best interest of Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall make a few comments on the legislation tabled in the House today, in which the Government is once again asking for borrowing authority, this time for nearly $30 billion.
I listened carefully to the Member for Rimouski (Mrs. Cote), and I noticed the depth of her concern for the problems facing young constituents in her riding. Our problems are the same. I was shocked when she mentioned an unemployment rate of 50 per cent, 22 per cent today, and of course I understand her comments and her concern for the problems facing this group. Mr. Speaker, when we hear that in the Hon. Member's riding alone, the federal Government spends $1 million a day on unemployment insurance and welfare, the
Hon. Member should realize, with respect, that this testifies to the Government's complete failure to take any kind of meaningful action. The Hon. Member has just confirmed and proved that over the past fifteen years, the economy has deteriorated to the extent that in her riding, it costs the Canadian Government $1 million a day to keep people on unemployment insurance and welfare. Mr. Speaker, may 1 remind the House that in 1969, on August 13, the Prime Minister said: "If we do nothing to slow down increases in expenditures, we are headed towards financial disaster." That is what the Prime Minister of Canada said in 1969. That is exactly the kind of disaster that was described by the Hon. Member for Rimouski, and I think that the concern that could be felt in the comments she made earlier is familiar to all or nearly all representatives of Canadian constituencies.
She is pleased to see that an agreement has been signed with the Quebec government whereby our young people who are on welfare and who must be satisfied with a pittance because jobs are non-existent will receive $150 more from the Federal government. She also said that from now on they will have a decent income of, I think, nearly $300 per month, that is, $75 per week.
I do not consider this as a decent income, Mr. Speaker. Not at all nor do I think that the hon. member for Rimouski would be satisfied with it. I am sure that she would rather see these young people, who are her constituents, with permanent jobs. Try as it might, the government could certainly not justify these $30 billion in borrowing powers on programs which are at best temporary, due to the devastating economic situation. That is why it is developing programs, Mr. Speaker, in view of the disastrous state of our economy. The Prime Minister, therefore, had foreseen a rise in government spending. But what has his government done since 1969, a time when it appeared so concerned about increases in spending? Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note what various people had to say about this. For instance, not so long ago, more specifically on January 12, 1980, the Prime Minister of Canada made the following statement: "We will maintain the rate of increase in government expenditures below the growth rate of our GNP, thereby decreasing gradually our deficit. All new spending programs set up to meet the changing needs of the Canadian people will be financed through a redistribution of current expenditures or revenue increases. We will not increase the deficit by setting up new programs". Thus spoke Pierre Elliott Trudeau, our current Prime Minister, on January 12, 1980.
Mr. Speaker, I quoted only two remarks from the Prime Minister, and yet we see what situation we are in. The government invokes now, just as it did in 1969, the need to reduce the deficit. Since then, we have had eight requests for borrowing power like today's request. We were successively asked for $ 12 billion, $14 billion, $6 billion, $4 billion, $19 billion and finally $29.5 billion. Mr. Speaker, as one of my colleagues put it, this
March 7, 1984

really borders on insolvency. Any individual who wants to borrow money from the bank must justify his request. There must be a climate of confidence. He is asked "How is business going?" These questions are asked today. The government is being accused, and with good reason, of being insolvent, irresponsible and hence incompetent. We know it full well, and Canadians are witness, they are worried regarding the growing per capita debt of Canadians, who are into debt for generations to come, Mr. Speaker, and you are aware of this as we all are.
The Government proves that it is unable to make both ends meet. They are asking us today for the eighth time to trust them and vote this borrowing authority bordering again on $30 billion. This is too much to ask, Mr. Speaker. It is too much to ask and most Canadians, according to surveys, no longer trust this Government, and they would surely blame us, and rightly so, for being remiss if we trusted the Government. However, this does not keep the Minister of Finance awake at night, as he stated last night, whether it be the value of the Canadian dollar or the deficit. It is obvious that the Minister of Finance will not spend sleepless nights because of what he considers as a small deficit. It is obvious that the Government has completely failed in terms of keeping its spending, as we ask, under tight control, in particular the spending of Crown corporations which do not hesitate to spend or even squander taxpayers' money and then, submit their deficit to Parliament. And the Government is wont to tell us that the indebtedness of Crown corporations is partly due to the House itself. That would not change anything, Mr. Speaker, and you know it. We get the bill at the end of the year and we cannot do anything about it, although people think we are responsible for the debts of Crown corporations and the way they squander public funds. Today, the Minister offhandedly brings before the House a piece of legislation and asks us to trust him. During all these years, the Government indebtedness has been steadily increasing. You know, Mr. Speaker, the Government reminds me of the chap who, in a hopeless situation, has to sell his stove to buy wood. There is not much difference, and the Government is sinking into debt. On January 12, 1980, the Prime Minister of Canada also accused the Conservatives of increasing by 100,000 the number of unemployed, but he added that the Liberals were going to bring it down, Mr. Speaker. Today, as you know, the Government in spite of countless efforts has to spend incredible sums of money to keep the 1,500,000 officially unemployed, and this does not include those whose claims have lapsed. We know that there are in fact 2 million people unemployed in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and that a good many of them are on welfare and will not even benefit from the agreement just signed relating to youth employment, because they are over 30 years old. At the dawn of the 1980s, we should not forget that the biggest challenge-I am still quoting the Prime Minister of Canada-"confronting our country is job creation, particularly for our young people."
To justify its expenditures, Mr. Speaker, the Government will obviously pride itself on having created thousands of jobs

last year, but these are temporary jobs and this fact will never be emphasized too much. These are temporary jobs only lasting for 20 to 26 weeks which means that these young people or not so young will have to claim unemployment insurance again and finally when their claims have lapsed, they will have to be satisfied with the meager pittance provided by welfare benefits. This has been an on-going process, Mr. Speaker. The Government has to borrow more money and therefore asks for additional borrowing powers. The following statistics, Mr. Speaker, speak for themselves; in all cases, they are reasonably adjusted. The number of unemployed in February 1980 was 874,000! In January, 1984, one million three hundred and seventy four thousand, that is, half a million more than anticipated. Youth unemployment: in February, 1980: 12.9 per cent; in February, 1984: 18.7 per cent, five per cent more, Mr. Speaker; 563,000 jobs have been lost during the recession, and the Canadian labour force is still 193,000 short, of what it was before this recession. The unemployment insurance scheme costs between $11 and $12 billion. This figure exceeds total expenditures made last year by the four Atlantic provinces governments combined.
When one looks at the debt and at this government's mismanagement for the past 15 years, Mr. Speaker, . . . The Prime Minister of Canada, who announced he would step down in the near future, obviously because he wanted to avoid being accused of this dismal failure, had predicted himself that this bankruptcy was bound to happen if we did not control government expenditures. They did not control their expenditures and we are on the verge of disaster, of bankruptcy. There is not a single businessman who would have put up with such bad managers for more than a few months; and Canadians have been putting up with them them for 16 years.
Given the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, you will understand that it is very difficult and indeed impossible for me to approve this request. This is a matter of confidence. And I cannot believe the Minister is introducing this bill as a normal piece of legislation. Bankruptcy after bankruptcy, and deficit after deficit. For years, we have been calling for adequate control of government expenditures by elected Members of this House, but to no avail. The Right Hon. Prime Minister and his ministers couldn't care less.
Given all this, you can logically expect us to reject this request by the Government. In fact, I believe we are not only right to do so, but it is our duty.
The Government proposes, Mr. Turner said on June 23, and I have met him before-

No, not Charles, John! The Government proposes, he said, to lead the way in terms of restraint by bringing its spending under tight control. At that time, that Minister of Finance had already introduced deficits, starting with a $5.5 billion deficit in 1975. All things considered, that deficit was quite similar to that proposed by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde)!
In his Budget, the then Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, stated on November 16, 1978: There can be no weakening in our determination to keep expenditu.es under tight control.
That is what the then Minister of Finance, who is now the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, said on November 16, 1979: that deficit was $12 billion!
On February 15, 1984, our present Minister of Finance said the following: . . . this budget is fiscally responsible. The time has come to control the expenses incurred by this Parliament: a deficit of $29 billion, Mr. Speaker! And the most recent figure is a deficit of $31 billion!
Would you say, Mr. Speaker, that this Government deserves the confidence of the Official Opposition for such mismanagement, and for what appears to be, even to those who hardly know how to count, such a sorry state of financial affairs? I think it is important that Canadians should realize that our national debt, which was approximately $10 or $15 billion fifteen years ago, has gone up to $150 billion. Mr. Speaker, in my mind, it is unthinkable for us to accept the invitation of this Government. Moreover, it is important and even essential for us to condemn this mismanagement and these shameful expenditures generally, this lack of control and this refusal on the Government's part to give back to this House some control, especially over Crown Corporations. Of course, Government expenditures have to be completely reassessed. We must also be given the controls we are requesting, and I have known this for at least ten years because that is how long we have known that under this Government our country was heading towards very serious financial difficulties. That is exactly what is happening, Mr. Speaker.
What is most incredible, when one listens to, and especially when one rereads the statements made by the various Ministers of Finance from Mr. Turner to this date, is the knowledge that this Government has literally deceived the population.
The Members opposite were elected after they had promised to control their expenditures, to reduce the deficit and consequently, to free certain amounts from the costs of financing the national debt. Now, the Government has the gall to ask us close to $30 billion and to tell us: "We only need $25 billion."
Their estimates having long been inaccurate, they mistrust their own projections. That is why they are asking $30 billion when admittedly they need only $25 billion. It is unthinkable, Mr. Speaker.
This is the reason why we will vote against such a confidence motion, because through this bill they are asking us to trust them. The public has lost all confidence in the management of this government and so has the Opposition, being in a better position to watch the actions of those responsible for government administration. They lost our confidence a long time ago, Mr. Speaker.
And since they would not support the measures we had been advocating in the best interest of Canada, to give this country more buoyancy through proper economic management, we will not agree to the request of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. It would be unthinkable, Mr. Speaker, because we cannot agree with a government which has failed so miserably. It is our duty to condemn this government and request elections as soon as possible for the simple reason that it has lost public confidence over the past 18 months, according to the polls.
And I do commend the Hon. Member for Rimouski-Temis-couata (Mrs. Cote) for her compassion towards her constituents. But, as a supporter of the scaring and harsh economic policies of this government, she cannot disclaim responsibility and is to be blamed for their plight. Canadians have started to realize that, and I hope they will let these Members know what they think of such mismanagement which has gone on too long, Mr. Speaker.
